title: Scalpel–Finger–Bougie Cricothyroidotomy
keywords: scalpel-finger-bougie technique — scalpel to make the hole, finger to keep it open and confirm you're in the trachea, bougie to railroad the tube over, no second-guessing the sequence
this is the last step of the difficult airway algorithm, decide early rather than as a final desperate move after everything else has failed
a 6.0 cuffed endotracheal tube is the standard railroad target, not a dedicated small cricothyroidotomy tube in the adult emergency scenario
vertical skin incision but a horizontal stab through the cricothyroid membrane itself
confirm with quantitative waveform capnography like any other airway
sources: Ahmad I, El-Boghdadly K, Bhagrath R, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2025 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. 2026;136(2):283-307 (vertical incision standardized for all necks; scalpel-bougie-tube; 3+1 / 3 / 2-person attempt ladder).

Frerk C, Mitchell VS, McNarry AF, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2015 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. 2015;115(6):827-848 (the superseded palpable/impalpable fork).

Cook TM, Woodall N, Frerk C. Major complications of airway management in the UK: 4th National Audit Project (NAP4). Br J Anaesth. 2011;106(5):617-631 (cannula cricothyroidotomy failed in roughly 60% of cases; surgical technique was near-uniformly successful).
Whatling J, et al. Adult front of neck airway: a narrative review. J Oral Maxillofac Anesth. 2024 (equipment rationale, complication profile, eFONA incidence ~1 in 50,000 UK general anesthetics).
Hill C, et al. Emergency surgical cricothyroidotomy: 24 case series and analysis of technique. J Emerg Med. 2018.
Brown CA, et al. Cricothyrotomy. In: The Walls Manual of Emergency Airway Management, 6th ed.

changelog.change: Added a landmark diagram to the positioning/identification step — first content use of the new declarative `diagram` block (common.schema.json#/$defs/diagram), rendered natively as SVG on web and SwiftUI Canvas on iOS. Original vector artwork, so there is no third-party image licensing and it works fully offline.

Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-15, fresh-look Batch 6). Previously only referenced as the terminal endpoint within the difficult-airway algorithm module without its own step-by-step procedure card, unlike other Procedures-section content of comparable acuity (central line, tube thoracostomy).

Rebuilt against DAS 2025 (Br J Anaesth 2026;136:283-307) and moved into the new CICO & Front-of-Neck Access category as the default adult technique. One substantive correction: v2 taught the DAS 2015 fork — stab incision if the membrane is palpable, vertical incision only if it is not. DAS 2025 deletes that fork and standardizes the midline vertical skin incision in EVERY neck, because palpation is unreliable even in good conditions and a decision point mid-crisis costs time. Equipment is now stated as a fixed set (size 10 blade, bougie, 6.0 cuffed tube) for the same reason. Added the attempt ladder that precedes the declaration, the laryngeal handshake, the ultrasound caveat, a dedicated impalpable-neck step, and an aftercare step.

Step 3 now shows the landmarks on a real neck: Gray's Anatomy plate 1195 (public domain) with the cricothyroid membrane, the midline, and the thyrohyoid-membrane trap called out in the caption. The schematic moved to step 4, where it shows what it was really about — the vertical skin incision and the transverse stab through the membrane.

purpose: The default adult emergency front-of-neck airway: scalpel, finger, bougie, tube. Updated to DAS 2025, which standardizes a midline VERTICAL skin incision in every neck and removes the palpable-versus-impalpable decision that used to sit in the middle of the procedure.
entryPrompt: The last step of the airway algorithm, and the one where hesitation is the main cause of death. Equipment is fixed so there is nothing to choose under pressure: a size 10 blade, a bougie, a 6.0 cuffed tube.

nodes.prompt: 1 · Declare it out loud, and commit
nodes.body:
Say the words: "This is CICO. I am doing a front-of-neck airway." It is a decision the whole team has to hear, not a private judgment — someone has to get the kit, someone has to stop the clock, and someone has to stop offering you another look with the laryngoscope.

DAS 2025 puts a hard ceiling on what comes before this moment, and the ceiling is a limit, not a quota — if an attempt is not obviously going to work, move on early rather than using up the allowance.

items: Plan A — tracheal intubation, videolaryngoscope first-line, a maximum of 3 + 1 attempts (the +1 being a more experienced operator).
Plan B — second-generation supraglottic airway, up to 3 attempts.
Plan C — two-person face-mask ventilation with adjuncts and optimal positioning. Treat failure here as the trigger for Plan D, not as something to persist with.
Plan D — declare CICO and go to the neck.

nodes.body:
The equipment is deliberately not a choice. DAS 2025 standardizes it because choosing under pressure makes people slower and worse: a scalpel with a SIZE 10 BLADE, a bougie, and a SIZE 6.0 cuffed tracheal tube. Nothing else is required, and a dedicated cricothyroidotomy kit is not needed.

Extend the neck unless the cervical spine forbids it — a roll or pillow under the shoulders drops the larynx into a usable position and, in women, measurably increases the height of the cricothyroid membrane. Keep oxygen flowing by whatever route is still working; a supraglottic airway left in place also improves membrane identification.

Stand on the patient's right if you are right-handed (left if left-handed), with the scalpel, bougie and tube laid out in the order you will pick them up.

nodes.prompt: 3 · Laryngeal handshake, then commit to the midline
nodes.body:
Stabilize the larynx with the non-dominant hand and use the LARYNGEAL HANDSHAKE: thumb and middle finger on the upper laryngeal cartilage, slide caudally to feel the thyroid laminae, then the cricoid ring, and identify the cricothyroid membrane as the soft depression between them.

Be honest about how often this fails. Misidentification is common — most of all in women and in patients with obesity — and the handshake is no more successful than plain palpation in pooled data, only slower. THAT IS WHY DAS 2025 NO LONGER ASKS YOU TO DECIDE based on what you can feel. Palpate to orient yourself, then cut regardless.

ULTRASOUND: only if a machine is already at the bedside and someone present can use it. It is better than palpation for finding the membrane in difficult anatomy, and it is the right tool BEFORE induction in a patient whose neck you cannot read. It is not something to send for during a CICO.

diagram.title: Cricothyroid membrane on a real neck
diagram.caption: The neck is extended, as it would be for the procedure. Coming down the midline you meet two soft gaps. The upper one, between the hyoid and the thyroid cartilage, is the thyrohyoid membrane — the wrong one. The target is the lower gap, between the bottom edge of the thyroid cartilage and the firm cricoid ring. This is a thin male neck with a visible prominence; in women and in patients with obesity these landmarks are far harder to feel, which is why the skin incision is vertical whatever you can palpate. Structure pointers are Gray's own leader lines; the target and midline are placed by hand on the engraving.

image.credit: Plate: Henry Vandyke Carter, Gray's Anatomy of the Human Body, 20th ed. (1918), fig. 1195 — public domain. Overlay: Kairos.

nodes.prompt: 4 · Vertical skin incision — in every neck
nodes.body:
Make a MIDLINE VERTICAL skin incision up to 8 cm long, cutting from caudad to cephalad (bottom to top). Go deep — through skin and subcutaneous tissue in one confident pass. Blood will obscure the field; that is expected and is not a reason to stop.

THIS IS THE CHANGE FROM DAS 2015, and it is worth knowing why you are doing it differently from how you may have been taught. The 2015 guideline asked you to choose: a transverse stab if you could feel the membrane, a vertical incision if you could not. DAS 2025 deletes the choice and makes vertical the standard for palpable and impalpable necks alike, for three reasons — palpation is unreliable even in controlled conditions, a decision point in the middle of a crisis slows you down, and a vertical incision exposes more of the airway either way. It also runs with the midline vessels rather than across them.

Then make a TRANSVERSE stab through the cricothyroid membrane itself, rotate the blade so the sharp edge faces caudally, and hold it there. The size 10 blade is chosen to limit damage to the posterior tracheal wall.

diagram.title: Vertical through the skin, transverse through the membrane
diagram.caption: Two cuts in two directions. The skin incision is vertical, in the midline, cut from bottom to top and long enough to admit a finger — it runs with the midline vessels rather than across them and exposes the airway whether or not you could feel the membrane. The membrane itself takes a transverse stab, then the blade is rotated so its sharp edge faces caudally.

nodes.prompt: 5 · If you still cannot find the membrane
nodes.body: Obesity, hematoma, radiotherapy change, prior surgery, subcutaneous emphysema — these are the necks where people die, and the technique does not change, only the amount of work between skin and airway.

items: Extend the vertical incision to 8-10 cm. You are trading a scar for an airway.

items.text: Put a finger in and dissect bluntly down the midline until you feel cartilage.
items: Sweep laterally with the finger to retract tissue, not to explore — the airway is in the midline and staying in the midline is the whole discipline.
Identify a firm ring. If you cannot tell membrane from cartilage, a stab through the ring below is survivable; a stab lateral to the midline is not.
If the anatomy is truly unrecognizable and ENT or surgery is physically present, a surgical tracheotomy is the better operation — but only if they are in the room now.

nodes.prompt: 6 · Finger — hold the tract, keep your place
nodes.body: The moment the membrane is open, put the index finger of the non-dominant hand into the incision. It does three jobs at once: it holds the tract open through tissue that wants to close, it confirms you are in the airway rather than a false passage, and it keeps your orientation while you put the scalpel down and pick up the bougie. Do not take it out until the bougie is in.

Slide the bougie along your finger, through the membrane, and into the trachea, angling caudally. A coudé (angled) tip helps it turn down rather than back. Advance roughly 10-15 cm.

Tracheal clicks over the rings, or hold-up at a distal bronchus, confirm you are in the airway. Their absence does not mean you have failed — in a bloody field with a short tract you often feel neither. Do not withdraw and start again on the strength of a missing click.

Railroad a well-lubricated size 6.0 cuffed tracheal tube over the bougie, rotating it if it catches at the skin. It is a standard tracheal tube, not a dedicated small-bore cricothyroidotomy tube — a 6.0 has an external diameter around 8.8 mm, which sits snugly with the cuff up in both male and female tracheas.

Advance only far enough to get the cuff past the membrane. This is a short airway and a right mainstem intubation is easy. Remove the bougie, inflate the cuff, ventilate.

nodes.prompt: 9 · Confirm the same way you would confirm any airway
nodes.body:
Quantitative waveform capnography. A surgical airway is not exempt from confirmation, and the most common reason an eFONA fails is that the device is in the wrong place rather than that the incision was wrong.

Secure it deliberately — this site dislodges far more easily than an oral tube, and it is held by tissue that is now bleeding and swelling. Recheck after every move of the patient.

nodes.prompt: 10 · Afterwards — it is a bridge, not a destination
nodes.body: Nothing about the next few hours is optional.

items: Get ENT or surgery involved for definitive airway planning — conversion to a formal tracheostomy or a controlled oral tube is a decision for after the crisis, not during it.
Imaging for the complications this procedure causes: pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, and esophageal or pharyngeal injury that can seed a mediastinal infection.

Document the attempt count at each plan, the time CICO was declared, the time the airway was secured, and what was found. This is how the next team knows what they are dealing with, and it is also how the unit learns.
Tell the patient and the family. Counsel about the longer-term risks — subglottic stenosis, tracheomalacia, tracheocutaneous fistula — and arrange follow-up.
Debrief the team. eFONA runs at roughly 1 in 50,000 general anesthetics; almost nobody gets a second one to learn from.

checklist: CICO declared out loud, and the team told that repeated intubation attempts have stopped
Size 10 blade, bougie, 6.0 cuffed tube — the fixed set, nothing to choose
Neck extended if the cervical spine allows; oxygen still flowing by some route
Midline VERTICAL skin incision up to 8 cm, in this neck regardless of what you could palpate
Transverse stab through the membrane, blade rotated sharp-edge-caudally
Finger in the tract before the scalpel goes down, and kept there until the bougie is in
Bougie railroaded along the finger, tube railroaded over the bougie, advanced only past the cuff
Quantitative waveform capnography before anyone relaxes
Tube secured hard, and rechecked after every patient move
ENT/surgery engaged, imaging obtained, times and attempt counts documented, team debriefed
buildNote: v3, DAS 2025 rebuild, and the anchor module of the new CICO & Front-of-Neck Access category. The substantive correction is the incision: v2 taught the DAS 2015 palpable/impalpable fork, which DAS 2025 deletes in favor of a vertical incision in every neck. The card says so explicitly rather than quietly changing, because most readers were trained on the old fork and need to know they are not misremembering. Sub-steps use the `substeps` structure rather than prose bullets. The intercostal-style diagram is carried over from v2 unchanged — the anatomy did not change, only the incision doctrine.
